evidence.label: A negatively pinched Kähler threefold without bounded holomorphic coordinates
One-sided negative sectional curvature and the holomorphic Liouville property

headline: Proves a complete Kähler threefold with pinched negative curvature can lack bounded holomorphic coordinates.
scope: A contractible domain in ℂ³ whose complete Kähler metric has curvatures between two negative constants. The companion works in some large fixed dimension.
plain: In one complex dimension, a complete, simply connected surface with curvature below a negative constant is the disc. In higher dimensions, experts asked if two-sided negative curvature forces bounded holomorphic coordinates, as on a bounded domain. The main paper builds a three-dimensional example where this fails, and Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal statement of it. A companion paper claims a stronger failure when only an upper curvature bound is kept: no nonconstant bounded holomorphic function at all.
doesNot: This does not settle whether two-sided pinching forces at least one nonconstant bounded holomorphic function; the main example has two. The companion's curvature is unbounded below, and it has no Lean check.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Hung-Hsi Wu, question (1) in his work on normal families
scorecard.significanceWhy: It answers a uniformization question of Wu and of Wu and Yau with a Lean-checked construction, and the companion claims Yau's one-sided problem.

explanation:
Take the unit disc, the complex numbers z with |z| < 1. Give it the Poincaré metric, which has constant curvature −1. The distance from the centre to the point r is 2 artanh r, which equals log((1 + r)/(1 − r)). At r = 0.9 this is log 19, about 2.944. At r = 0.99 it is log 199, about 5.293. As r nears 1 the distance grows without limit, so the metric is complete: the edge is infinitely far away. Yet the coordinate z itself stays smaller than 1. So the disc has a bounded holomorphic coordinate, a bounded function given by a complex power series.

In complex dimension one, a complete simply connected surface with curvature below a negative constant is the disc[2]. In higher dimensions, Wu asked a similar question. Wu and Yau stated a two-sided version[3]. Suppose a complete simply connected Kähler manifold has every curvature between two negative constants. Must it be a bounded domain, so that it has bounded holomorphic coordinates? A Kähler manifold is a complex space with a metric that fits its complex structure. Mostow and Siu found examples not covered by the ball, but those did not rule out some other bounded domain[4].

The first paper proves the answer is no. It builds a contractible domain in ℂ³ with a complete Kähler metric whose curvatures lie between −B and −A, both negative. No bounded holomorphic map to ℂ³ has a nowhere-zero Jacobian, so the domain is not a bounded domain[1]. The space is a family of discs over the unit ball in ℂ². The disc above z has radius e^(−φ(z)/2) for a chosen function φ[5]. The obstacle is to pick φ smooth enough for curvature control, yet rough enough to block every bounded holomorphic coordinate. The example still has two nonconstant bounded holomorphic functions, its base coordinates[6].

The second paper drops the lower curvature bound. In some large fixed complex dimension, it claims a domain with curvature at most −1 and only constant bounded holomorphic functions[7]. This answers the one-sided question, which Wu and Yau trace to Yau's Problem 38 from 1982[8]. Its curvature is unbounded below[9]. The two constructions and their proofs are independent[10].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal statement of the first paper's main result. So that paper proves its construction, as far as the Lean statement matches the paper. The companion's one-sided result is not in the Lean scope and remains a claim. No specialist review of either paper is published.
hypeCheck: Major for the first result, which has a Lean statement and answers a stated uniformization question. The one-sided companion is a claim without a Lean check. Neither paper has a published specialist review.
